faq.a: Staphylococcus aureus, often methicillin‑sensitive but MRSA is increasingly common.
faq.q: What is the most common organism causing breast abscess in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: Yes, especially in HIV‑positive patients; look for systemic TB symptoms and confirm with GeneXpert or culture.
faq.q: Can breast inflammation be a sign of tuberculosis?

faq.a: When the abscess is >5 cm, multiloculated, or not responding to antibiotics within 48–72 h.

exam: What is the first line antibiotic for a diabetic patient with suspected Staph aureus breast abscess? — Use cloxacillin or dicloxacillin; avoid fluoroquinolones in diabetics due to tendon risk.
ai.title: Breast Inflammation
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Acute or chronic inflammation of breast tissue, often due to infection or abscess, presenting with pain, redness, swelling, and sometimes drainage. Diagnosis relies on history, exam, and basic imaging or cultures, with management tailored to the underlying cause.

b: Possible nipple discharge or sinus tracts
sections.p: Breast inflammation is the host response to injury or infection, characterised by pain, erythema, warmth, and sometimes purulent drainage. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by simple imaging or culture if available.

t.b: Fluid collection suggests abscess; normal imaging favours cellulitis
Staph aureus most common; MRSA prevalence high in some areas

sections.p: Staging follows the WHO breast abscess classification: Stage 1 – superficial cellulitis; Stage 2 – localized abscess <5 cm; Stage 3 – large or multiloculated abscess; Stage 4 – systemic sepsis.

b: Malaria or schistosomiasis – rarely cause secondary inflammation
sections.p: In East Africa, the top causes are bacterial mastitis (often Staph aureus), tuberculosis of the breast, and fungal infections in immunocompromised patients.
Patients report sudden breast pain, redness, and swelling. In advanced stages, a fluctuant mass or draining sinus may be seen. Systemic signs like fever and malaise indicate severe disease.

b: TB skin test or GeneXpert – if TB suspected
sections.p: Investigation choice depends on resource availability. Basic labs, imaging, and cultures guide treatment.
Severe pain, rapidly enlarging mass, high fever, tachycardia, or signs of sepsis require urgent referral.

b: Avoid fluoroquinolones in children and pregnant women
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor closely. Antibiotics are chosen based on likely organisms and local resistance patterns.

b: Vaccinate against influenza to reduce secondary infections
sections.p: Patients should be reassessed within 48–72 h. Prevention focuses on hygiene, early treatment of infections, and managing diabetes.
Differential includes breast carcinoma, granulomatous mastitis, and breast abscess secondary to trauma.

b: Ultrasound false negative if operator inexperienced
sections.p: Normal white cell count does not exclude infection; low CRP can occur in early disease. Ultrasound may miss small abscesses.

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock, sudden increase in pain or size, high fever >39 °C, altered consciousness
